items.problem: Your team copies information between tools, follows up manually, or cannot see where work gets stuck.
items.approach: Connect existing systems through APIs, automate repeatable steps, and add AI where a human can review the result.
items.result: Less duplicate entry, clear ownership of exceptions, and a workflow the team can monitor.
items.example: A new enquiry enters a shared pipeline, is assigned to an owner, and creates a follow-up task. Unclear requests go to a person.

items.problem: Customers, partners, or staff need one place to manage a process with different roles and permissions.
items.approach: Design the data model, role-based dashboards, account journeys, and the APIs that connect the platform to your operations.
items.result: People can complete their task, find the right information, and understand what happens next.
items.example: Recruitment operations: candidate records, interview scheduling, and document workflows, as shown in Qianlima.

items.problem: Your website makes your offer difficult to understand or creates friction between interest and enquiry.
items.approach: Plan the information structure, build responsive pages and product flows, and connect content management or commerce where needed.
items.result: Clear service information, accessible navigation, and an enquiry path that works on phones as well as desktops.
items.example: A local service website explains its coverage and services, then gives customers a direct route to ask for help.

items.problem: Your brand and interface change from page to page, making the product harder to recognize and use.
items.approach: Create a visual identity, shared interface patterns, and reusable design components for your website or product.
items.result: A consistent experience with practical rules your team can apply as the product grows.
items.example: One system for typography, color, buttons, forms, and feedback across public pages and account dashboards.

items.problem: You publish content or run campaigns without a reliable view of which journeys lead to meaningful enquiries.
items.approach: Set up technical SEO, content structures, and purposeful analytics events around the enquiry journey.
items.result: A clearer view of where visitors continue or drop off, with a basis for testing improvements.
items.example: Track service views, contact starts, and successful enquiries without putting personal form details into analytics.

items.problem: You know a process needs to improve, but the requirements and first useful release are still unclear.
items.approach: Map the current workflow, identify users and constraints, prototype important steps, and prioritize a delivery roadmap.
items.result: An agreed problem, a manageable first scope, and clear acceptance criteria before a larger build.
items.example: Map an approval process, identify who can decide at each step, and prototype the handoff before choosing tools.

workflow.label: A connected workflow
workflow.heading: From a request to a clear next action
workflow.description: An example of how the tools your team already uses can work together. The starting point is a real process and the people responsible for it.

steps.title: Receive
steps.body: A form, inbox, or existing system captures the request.

steps.title: Connect
steps.body: Check the information and pass it to the right record or tool.

steps.title: Review
steps.body: A person handles approvals, missing details, and exceptions.

steps.title: Act & learn
steps.body: Create the next task and make its status visible to the team.

workflow.note: Start with one useful workflow. Keep human review where the decision needs judgment.

process.heading: How we work together
process.description: Start with the operational problem, then agree on a practical first release and what it needs to prove.

steps.title: Understand
steps.body: Walk through the current process, users, tools, and points where work slows down.

steps.title: Define
steps.body: Agree on scope, responsibilities, priorities, and acceptance criteria before committing to a build.

steps.title: Build & review
steps.body: Develop the experience and connected workflows, then review them against real user tasks.

steps.title: Launch & hand over
steps.body: Plan release checks, documentation, access, and the support responsibilities included in your scope.

items.question: What does an operations audit start with?
items.answer: Share one process that is slow or repetitive, the tools involved, and the result you want. We can use that context to discuss the bottleneck and a suitable next step. The depth, deliverables, timing, and fee for any audit are agreed before work starts.

items.question: Do we need a finished brief or a chosen technology?
items.answer: No. Start with the problem, who experiences it, and how the process works today. Existing tools and constraints help shape the scope; you do not need to choose a platform first.

items.question: How are cost and delivery time decided?
items.answer: They depend on the workflows, integrations, content, and review requirements. Ask for a scoped proposal with milestones, assumptions, and what is included before committing.

items.question: Can you work with our existing systems?
items.answer: Integration is part of our services. Compatibility depends on available APIs, access, data quality, and the rules of each system. These should be checked during discovery.

items.question: Who owns the accounts, code, and content?
items.answer: Ownership, licenses, account access, and handover arrangements should be explicit in your proposal and agreement. Raise any existing supplier or hosting constraints before the build begins.

items.question: What happens after launch?
items.answer: Agree on documentation, training, bug fixes, maintenance, and response expectations as part of the scope. Ongoing support and future features should be defined clearly rather than assumed.

guide.label: Practical guide
guide.title: Before you automate: map one workflow
guide.description: A short checklist to identify a useful first automation, the exceptions it must handle, and what success should mean.
guide.intro: Start with a task people already do. A clear map of the current process makes it easier to choose what to automate, what to keep manual, and what to measure.

steps.title: Choose one repeatable task
steps.body: Pick a specific starting point and finishing point. “A new enquiry arrives and gets an owner” is easier to scope than “automate sales.” Note who does the work and how often it happens.

steps.title: Write down the current handoffs
steps.body: List each tool, the information entering it, and the person responsible for the next step. Include spreadsheets, messages, and the informal checks that make the process work today.

steps.title: Record the exceptions
steps.body: What happens when information is missing, a request is duplicated, or someone does not respond? Decide who handles these cases. A useful automation needs a visible recovery path.

steps.title: Decide where people stay involved
steps.body: Keep a person responsible for decisions that need judgment. If AI drafts or classifies information, define how someone reviews it and corrects a mistake before it triggers a consequential action.

steps.title: Define a small success measure
steps.body: Record a baseline such as handling time, duplicate entry, or missed follow-ups. Choose one or two measures you can compare after a pilot. Avoid promising a result before you have evidence.

steps.title: Test a limited pilot
steps.body: Use a small, agreed set of cases. Check normal requests and exceptions, confirm access rules, and define how to pause the workflow. Review the results with the people who use it before expanding.

guide.example: A website form creates a shared record. A rule assigns an owner, and a task reminds them to follow up. Missing information goes to a review queue. The team checks unassigned enquiries and completed follow-ups to see whether the change helps.
